## Question 122: A Confidence Interval and Test for a Poisson Sighting Rate

::: {.exam-prompt}

At the Council of Elrond, scouts bring reports from the lands around Isengard. For each of $n$
consecutive days, riders from Rohan record the number of enemy war-parties seen near the Gap of
Rohan. Let $X_i$ denote the count on day $i$, and suppose $$
X_1,\ldots,X_n \stackrel{\mathrm{iid}}{\sim} \mathrm{Poisson}(\lambda),
$$ where $\lambda > 0$ is the (unknown) mean number of sightings per day.

In earlier, quieter times, the rate was believed to be about $\lambda = 1$ sighting per day. The
Council now wishes to assess whether enemy activity has increased.

(a) Show that the maximum likelihood estimator (MLE) of $\lambda$ is $$
    \hat{\lambda} = \bar{X} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n X_i.
    $$ Compute $\mathrm{E}[\hat{\lambda}]$ and $\mathrm{Var}(\hat{\lambda})$. [\[3 marks\]]{.exam-part-marks}

(b) (i) Using the Central Limit Theorem (CLT), state an approximate distribution for $\hat{\lambda}$
        when $n$ is large. [\[2 marks\]]{.exam-part-marks}

    (ii) Hence write down an approximate $100(1-\alpha)\%$ confidence interval for $\lambda$ in
         terms of $\hat{\lambda}$, $n$ and the normal quantile $z_{1-\alpha/2}$. [\[2 marks\]]{.exam-part-marks}

(c) In one set of reports, the scouts observe $n = 36$ days and a total of $$
    \sum_{i=1}^{36} x_i = 90
    $$ enemy war-parties near the Gap of Rohan.

    Using the CLT approximation, test $H_0:\lambda = 1$ against the one-sided alternative
    $H_1:\lambda > 1$ at the 5% significance level.

    State clearly whether $H_0$ should be rejected, and briefly interpret your conclusion in the
    context of the safety of the route past Isengard. [\[3 marks\]]{.exam-part-marks}

You may use the standard Normal quantile $z_{0.95} = 1.645$.

:::

<details class="solution">
  <summary>Solution</summary>

(a) By independence, the log-likelihood is
    $$
    \ell(\lambda;\underline x)=-n\lambda+\left(\sum_{i=1}^n x_i\right)\log\lambda
    -\sum_{i=1}^n\log(x_i!).
    $$
    If the sample total is positive, setting the derivative
    $-n+\big(\sum_{i=1}^n x_i\big)/\lambda$ to zero gives the MLE $\hat\lambda=\bar X$.
    If all counts are zero, $\bar X=0$ gives the boundary estimate in the usual model allowing
    $\lambda=0$. In the strictly positive parameter space the likelihood has its supremum
    as $\lambda\downarrow0$. Using the Poisson mean and variance and independence gives
    $$
    \mathrm{E}[\bar X]=\lambda,\qquad
    \mathrm{Var}(\bar X)=\frac{\lambda}{n}.
    $$

(b) (i) By the CLT, $\hat\lambda$ is approximately $\mathcal N(\lambda,\lambda/n)$ for large $n$.

    (ii) Replacing $\lambda$ by $\hat\lambda$ in the standard error gives the approximate
         $100(1-\alpha)\%$ confidence interval
         $$
         \hat\lambda\ \pm\ z_{1-\alpha/2}\sqrt{\frac{\hat\lambda}{n}}.
         $$

(c) Here $\hat\lambda=90/36=2.5$. Under $H_0$, the CLT gives
    $Z=(\hat\lambda-1)/\sqrt{1/36}\overset{\mathrm{approx.}}{\sim}\mathcal N(0,1)$.
    The observed $z$ is $(2.5-1)/(1/6)=9$. Since $9>1.645$, reject $H_0$ at the 5% level.
    The data support an increase in the mean rate of sightings near the route, suggesting
    greater danger to travellers.

</details>

## Question 123: Likelihood and Bayesian Inference for Negative Binomial Counts

::: {.exam-prompt}

In the garden of Lothlórien, Galadriel invites Frodo to gaze into her Mirror. The Mirror displays a
continuous sequence of visions. Due to the shifting nature of time, any single vision is either a
*Vision of the Future* (with unknown probability $p$) or a fleeting *Reflection of the Past* (with
probability $1-p$).

Frodo watches the Mirror until he has witnessed exactly $r$ Visions of the Future. Let $X$ denote
the number of Reflections of the Past he observes before the $r$-th Vision of the Future appears.
The distribution of $X$ is modelled as $$
X \sim \mathrm{NegBin}(r,p),
$$ with probability mass function $$
\Pr(X = x \mid p)
= \binom{x + r - 1}{r - 1}
  p^r (1-p)^x,
\qquad x = 0,1,2,\ldots,
$$ where $0 < p < 1$. It can be shown that $$
\mathrm{E}[X] = \frac{r(1-p)}{p},
\qquad
\mathrm{Var}(X) = \frac{r(1-p)}{p^2}.
$$

Galadriel asks Frodo to repeat this trial on $n$ different occasions (assume these attempts are
independent). On each occasion, Frodo watches the Mirror until he has witnessed $r$ Visions of the
Future, and records $X_i$, the number of Reflections of the Past observed before the $r$-th Vision
appears. The resulting observations are $X_1,\ldots,X_n$. Assume at least one is positive.

(a) Show that the maximum likelihood estimator $\hat{p}$ of $p$ is given by $$
    \hat{p}
    = \frac{r}{r + \bar{X}},
    \qquad \text{where } \bar{X} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n X_i.
    $$ [\[6 marks\]]{.exam-part-marks}

(b) For a single observation $X \sim \mathrm{NegBin}(r,p)$, show that the second derivative of the
    log-likelihood (with respect to $p$) can be written as $$
    \frac{\partial^2}{\partial p^2} \log f(X \mid p)
    = -\,\frac{X}{(1-p)^2} - \frac{r}{p^2}.
    $$

    Hence show that the Fisher information for a single observation is $$
    \mathcal{I}_1(p)
    = \frac{r}{p^2(1-p)},
    $$ and deduce the Fisher information $\mathcal{I}_n(p)$ for the full sample. [\[5 marks\]]{.exam-part-marks}

(c) Galadriel possesses ancient wisdom regarding the clarity of the Mirror. She places a
    $\mathrm{Beta}(\alpha,\beta)$ prior on $p$, with density $$
    \pi(p) \propto p^{\alpha-1}(1-p)^{\beta-1}, \qquad 0 < p < 1.
    $$

    (i) Show that the posterior distribution for $p$ given the data $x_1,\dots,x_n$ is $$
        p \mid x_1,\dots,x_n
        \sim \mathrm{Beta}\big(\alpha + nr,\; \beta + S\big),
        \qquad \text{where } S = \sum_{i=1}^n x_i.
        $$ [\[4 marks\]]{.exam-part-marks}

    (ii) Hence write down the posterior mean and variance of $p$.

         Using your expression for $$
         \mathcal{I}_n(p)
         $$ from part (b), derive the *asymptotic posterior distribution* for $p$.

         Comment on the connection between the Bayesian posterior and the frequentist large-sample
         distribution of the MLE. [\[5 marks\]]{.exam-part-marks}

:::

<details class="solution">
  <summary>Solution</summary>

**(a)** Let $S=\sum_i x_i$. By independence, the likelihood is
$$
L(p;\underline{x})
=p^{nr}(1-p)^S\prod_{i=1}^n\binom{x_i+r-1}{r-1}.
$$
Its log has derivative $nr/p-S/(1-p)$. Equating this to zero gives the estimate
$nr/(nr+S)$. Because $S>0$, the solution is interior, and strict concavity gives a maximum.
Writing the result in terms of the random sample yields
$$
\hat{p}=\frac{r}{r+\bar{X}}.
$$

**(b)** For a single observation the terms in the log-likelihood that depend on $p$ are
$r\log p+X\log(1-p)$. Differentiating twice gives $-r/p^2-X/(1-p)^2$. Using the stated
mean of $X$, the information is
$$
\mathcal{I}_1(p)=\frac{r}{p^2}+\frac{\mathrm{E}[X]}{(1-p)^2}
=\frac{r}{p^2}+\frac{r}{p(1-p)}
=\frac{r}{p^2(1-p)}.
$$
The log-likelihoods add over independent observations, so
$\mathcal{I}_n(p)=nr/[p^2(1-p)]$.

**(c)(i)** Multiplying likelihood and prior gives
$$
\pi(p\mid\underline{x})\propto
p^{\alpha+nr-1}(1-p)^{\beta+S-1}.
$$
The posterior is therefore $\mathrm{Beta}(a,b)$ with $a=\alpha+nr$ and $b=\beta+S$.

**(c)(ii)** The posterior mean and variance are
$$
\mathrm{E}[p\mid\underline{x}]=\frac{a}{a+b},
\qquad
\mathrm{Var}(p\mid\underline{x})=\frac{ab}{(a+b)^2(a+b+1)}.
$$
The prior parameters are fixed, so for large $n$ the posterior mean $a/(a+b)$ is close to
$\hat{p}=nr/(nr+S)$ and $a+b+1$ is close to $nr+S=nr/\hat{p}$. Writing the posterior variance
as $[a/(a+b)][b/(a+b)]/(a+b+1)$ gives a leading term of
$\hat{p}^{\,2}(1-\hat{p})/(nr)$, the inverse Fisher information at $\hat{p}$.
The resulting Normal approximation is
$$
p\mid\underline{x}\overset{\text{approx.}}{\sim}
\mathcal{N}\!\left(\hat{p},\,\frac{\hat{p}^{\,2}(1-\hat{p})}{nr}\right).
$$
In the frequentist sampling distribution, $\hat{p}$ is random and centred approximately at the
true $p_0$, with approximate variance $p_0^2(1-p_0)/(nr)$. Both approximations use inverse
Fisher information. The posterior treats the data as fixed and uses $\hat p$ for its centre and
variance calculation.

</details>

## Question 124: Gamma–Poisson Updating for Orc Sightings

::: {.exam-prompt}

On the eastern bank of the Anduin, beyond the borders of Gondor, Faramir's Rangers observe raiding
parties of orcs moving along the river. Let $X_i$ denote the number of orcs sighted in the $i$th
raiding party (crossing a fixed stretch of riverbank) during a scouting mission. Suppose that,
conditional on the unknown average orc intensity $\lambda > 0$, $$
X_1,\ldots,X_n \mid \lambda \stackrel{\mathrm{iid}}{\sim} \mathrm{Poisson}(\lambda).
$$

The Rangers, trained in the interpretation of scouting reports, model $\lambda$ using a conjugate
prior, $$
\lambda \sim \mathrm{Gamma}(\alpha_0,\beta_0).
$$

(a) (i) Write down the likelihood $L(\lambda; \underline{x})$ and show that $$
        L(\lambda; \underline{x}) \propto \lambda^{n\bar{x}} e^{-n\lambda}.
        $$ [\[3 marks\]]{.exam-part-marks}

    (ii) Using the prior $\lambda \sim \mathrm{Gamma}(\alpha_0,\beta_0)$, show that the posterior
         distribution takes the form $$
         \lambda \mid \underline{x} \sim \mathrm{Gamma}(\alpha_0 + n\bar{x}, \, \beta_0+n).
         $$ [\[3 marks\]]{.exam-part-marks}

(b) Across $n = 10$ observed raiding parties, the Rangers record a total of $243$ orcs: $$
    \sum_{i=1}^n x_i = 243.
    $$ Suppose the Rangers choose prior parameters $\alpha_0 = 3$ and $\beta_0 = 0.25$.

    (i) Write down the posterior distribution of $\lambda \mid \underline{x}$ and compute the
        posterior mean. [\[2 marks\]]{.exam-part-marks}

    (ii) Compute the posterior variance $\mathrm{Var}(\lambda \mid \underline{x})$ under the
         posterior from part (b)(i). Comment briefly on whether the captains of Gondor are justified
         in judging that the western bank is in grave danger if the expected orc count per raiding
         party exceeds $15$. [\[3 marks\]]{.exam-part-marks}

(c) Denethor, Steward of Gondor, refuses to accept growing signs of danger. Influenced by dark
    visions from the palantír, he insists that even after receiving the Rangers' reports, the
    *expected* orc count per raiding party is at most $15$, that is $$
    \mathrm{E}[\lambda \mid \underline{x}] \le 15.
    $$

    Assume Denethor also uses a Gamma prior, $$
    \lambda \sim \mathrm{Gamma}(\alpha_D,\beta_D),
    $$ but with unknown parameters $\alpha_D,\beta_D > 0$.

    Using the form of the posterior from part (a)(ii), derive a condition on $(\alpha_D,\beta_D)$
    which must hold if $$
    \mathrm{E}[\lambda \mid \underline{x}] \le 15
    $$ under Denethor's posterior. [\[5 marks\]]{.exam-part-marks}

(d) Briefly explain how Denethor's prior $\mathrm{Gamma}(\alpha_D,\beta_D)$ must differ from the
    Rangers' prior $\mathrm{Gamma}(\alpha_0,\beta_0)$ to maintain such denial after seeing the same
    evidence. [\[4 marks\]]{.exam-part-marks}

:::

<details class="solution">
  <summary>Solution</summary>

**(a)(i)** The Poisson likelihood for independent observations is
$$
L(\lambda;\underline{x})
=\prod_{i=1}^n\frac{e^{-\lambda}\lambda^{x_i}}{x_i!}
=\frac{\lambda^{n\bar{x}} e^{-n\lambda}}{\prod_{i=1}^n x_i!}
\propto \lambda^{n\bar{x}}e^{-n\lambda}.
$$

**(a)(ii)** Using the Gamma prior with shape $\alpha_0$ and rate $\beta_0$, the posterior kernel
is
$$
\pi(\lambda\mid\underline{x})\propto
\lambda^{\alpha_0+n\bar{x}-1}e^{-(\beta_0+n)\lambda}.
$$
Thus $\lambda\mid\underline{x}\sim\mathrm{Gamma}(\alpha_0+n\bar{x},\beta_0+n)$.

**(b)(i)** The updated parameters are $3+243=246$ and $0.25+10=10.25$. The posterior
is $\mathrm{Gamma}(246,10.25)$ with mean $246/10.25=24$.

**(b)(ii)** The posterior variance is $246/10.25^2\approx 2.341$. The posterior mean count
of $24$ exceeds the threshold of $15$ and the posterior standard deviation is about $1.53$.
The captains' assessment is supported by these data and the Rangers' prior.

**(c)** Denethor's posterior is $\mathrm{Gamma}(\alpha_D+243,\beta_D+10)$. Its mean satisfies
$$
\frac{\alpha_D+243}{\beta_D+10}\le 15
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
15\beta_D-\alpha_D\ge 93.
$$

**(d)** Write $m_D=\alpha_D/\beta_D$ for Denethor's prior mean. The condition becomes
$\beta_D(15-m_D)\ge 93$. He needs a prior mean below $15$ and a prior weight $\beta_D$
of at least $93/(15-m_D)$ to offset the data. Since $m_D>0$, this requires $\beta_D>6.2$,
compared with the Rangers' weight of $0.25$. For example, he could share their prior mean of
$12$ by taking $\beta_D=31$ and $\alpha_D=372$, which gives a posterior mean of exactly $15$.

</details>

## Question 125: Sequential Beta–Bernoulli Updating for Riddle Outcomes

::: {.exam-prompt}

Deep in the Misty Mountains, Gollum challenges Bilbo Baggins to a game of riddles. For each riddle
$t=1,2,3$, define $$
X_t =
\begin{cases}
1, & \text{if Bilbo answers riddle } t \text{ correctly},\\[3pt]
0, & \text{if he answers incorrectly}.
\end{cases}
$$

From Gollum's perspective, Bilbo has an unknown *riddle-ability* $\theta \in (0,1)$, and $$
\Pr(X_t = 1 \mid \theta) = \theta, \qquad t=1,2,3,
$$ with the riddle outcomes independent given $\theta$.

Gollum, believing Bilbo to be unlikely to survive a riddle contest, chooses the prior $$
\theta \sim \mathrm{Beta}(\alpha_0,\beta_0), \qquad \alpha_0 = 1,\;\beta_0 = 9.
$$

He then observes the outcomes of three riddles:

-   Riddle 1 (fairly easy): Bilbo answers correctly ($X_1 = 1$).

-   Riddle 2 (somewhat tricky): Bilbo answers correctly ($X_2 = 1$).

-   Riddle 3 (a very difficult riddle): Bilbo answers correctly ($X_3 = 1$).

(a) Compute the prior mean of $\theta$ under the $\mathrm{Beta}(1,9)$ distribution and briefly
    interpret this from Gollum's perspective. [\[2 marks\]]{.exam-part-marks}

(b) Using the Beta--Bernoulli conjugate update, derive Gollum's posterior distribution for $\theta$:

    (i) after observing $X_1 = 1$ only;

    (ii) after observing $X_1 = 1$ and $X_2 = 1$;

    (iii) after observing all three riddles: $X_1 = 1$, $X_2 = 1$, $X_3 = 1$.

    Give each posterior in $\mathrm{Beta}(\alpha,\beta)$ form with updated parameters. [\[6 marks\]]{.exam-part-marks}

(c) Although Gollum views Riddle 3 as far more difficult than the others, the Beta--Bernoulli model
    treats all riddles identically. Briefly comment on this modelling assumption: does the model
    adequately represent Gollum's beliefs about riddle difficulty? [\[2 marks\]]{.exam-part-marks}

:::

<details class="solution">
  <summary>Solution</summary>

(a) The prior mean is $1/(1+9)=0.10$. Before seeing the answers, Gollum expects Bilbo to have a
    10% chance of answering any given riddle correctly under his model.

(b) With $k$ successes in $m$ independent riddles, the likelihood kernel is
    $\theta^k(1-\theta)^{m-k}$. Multiplying by the $\mathrm{Beta}(\alpha_0,\beta_0)$ prior
    density gives
    $$
    \pi(\theta\mid\underline x)
    \propto \theta^{\alpha_0+k-1}(1-\theta)^{\beta_0+m-k-1}.
    $$
    Hence each correct answer adds one to the first shape parameter and each incorrect
    answer adds one to the second. All the answers here are correct.

    (i) $\theta\mid X_1=1\sim\mathrm{Beta}(2,9)$.

    (ii) $\theta\mid X_1=X_2=1\sim\mathrm{Beta}(3,9)$.

    (iii) $\theta\mid X_1=X_2=X_3=1\sim\mathrm{Beta}(4,9)$.

(c) The model gives every riddle the same conditional success probability $\theta$ and therefore
    gives every correct answer the same weight. Representing Gollum's belief about difficulty
    would require the success probability to depend on the riddle as well as Bilbo's ability.

</details>

## Question 126: Gaussian Likelihood Ratio Test for a Trend in Echo Intensity

::: {.exam-prompt}

As the Fellowship travels through the Mines of Moria, Gandalf periodically halts the Company to
listen for distant echoes of orc movement. At each listening point $i = 1,\ldots,n$, taken $t_i$
hours after entering the mines, he assigns a numerical intensity $Y_i$ to the sound he hears.

Because echo measurements fluctuate randomly, Gandalf models them as $$
Y_i \sim \mathcal{N}(\beta t_i,\, \sigma^2),
$$ independently, where $\sigma^2$ is known and $\beta$ is an unknown constant. Here $\beta$
represents the *rate of change* of echo intensity over time.

Gandalf wishes to test whether the echoes are changing in intensity: $$
H_0 : \beta = 0
\qquad\text{vs.}\qquad
H_1 : \beta \neq 0.
$$

(a) Write down the likelihood function $L(\beta)$ and the log-likelihood $\ell(\beta)$. By
    differentiating $\ell(\beta)$ and setting the derivative to zero, show that the maximum
    likelihood estimator of $\beta$ is $$
    \hat{\beta}
    = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^n t_i Y_i}{\sum_{i=1}^n t_i^2}.
    $$ [\[6 marks\]]{.exam-part-marks}

(b) The likelihood ratio statistic is $$
    \Lambda = \frac{L(\beta=0)}{L(\hat{\beta})}.
    $$

    (i) Show that $$
        -2\log\Lambda
        = \frac{1}{\sigma^2}
        \left(
          \sum_{i=1}^n Y_i^2
          - \sum_{i=1}^n (Y_i - \hat{\beta} t_i)^2
        \right).
        $$ [\[4 marks\]]{.exam-part-marks}

    (ii) State the approximate sampling distribution of $-2\log\Lambda$ under $H_0$ (you may quote
         the likelihood ratio theorem), and hence give an approximate size-$\alpha$ rejection
         region. [\[3 marks\]]{.exam-part-marks}

(c) During one stretch of tunnels, the Fellowship takes $n=10$ measurements at times
    $t_i = 0,1,2,\dots,9$, using a known $\sigma^2 = 1$. Gandalf computes $$
    \hat{\beta} \approx 0.1373,
    \qquad
    -2\log\Lambda = 5.37.
    $$

    At the $5\%$ significance level, carry out the test and state whether the Fellowship should
    reject $H_0$. [\[4 marks\]]{.exam-part-marks}

(d) Briefly interpret your conclusion in the context of the journey through Moria. What would a
    non-zero $\beta$ indicate about the dangers ahead? [\[3 marks\]]{.exam-part-marks}

You may use the chi-squared quantile $\chi^2_{1,0.95} = 3.841$.

:::

<details class="solution">
  <summary>Solution</summary>

**(a)** By independence, the likelihood and log-likelihood for observed values $y_i$ are
$$
\begin{aligned}
L(\beta)&=(2\pi\sigma^2)^{-n/2}
\exp\!\left\{-\frac{1}{2\sigma^2}\sum_{i=1}^n(y_i-\beta t_i)^2\right\},\\
\ell(\beta)&=-\frac{n}{2}\log(2\pi\sigma^2)
-\frac{1}{2\sigma^2}\sum_{i=1}^n(y_i-\beta t_i)^2.
\end{aligned}
$$
Differentiating gives $\ell'(\beta)=\sigma^{-2}\sum_i t_i(y_i-\beta t_i)$.
Let $D=\sum_i t_i^2$. With $D>0$, setting the derivative to zero gives
$\hat{\beta}=\sum_i t_iY_i/D$. Since $\ell''(\beta)=-D/\sigma^2<0$, this is a maximum.

**(b)(i)** The log likelihood ratio is $\log\Lambda=\ell(0)-\ell(\hat{\beta})$.
The constant cancels, giving
$$
-2\log\Lambda
=2\{\ell(\hat{\beta})-\ell(0)\}
=\frac{1}{\sigma^2}
\left[\sum_iY_i^2-\sum_i(Y_i-\hat{\beta}t_i)^2\right].
$$

**(b)(ii)** The likelihood ratio theorem gives an approximate $\chi_1^2$ null distribution
because the restriction $\beta=0$ removes one parameter. Reject $H_0$ when
$-2\log\Lambda>\chi^2_{1,1-\alpha}$. In this model the null distribution is in fact exact.
Expanding the square in part (b)(i) and using $\sum_i t_iY_i=D\hat{\beta}$ gives
$-2\log\Lambda=D\hat{\beta}^{\,2}/\sigma^2$. Under $H_0$,
$\hat{\beta}$ is Normal with mean zero and variance $\sigma^2/D$, so the statistic is the square
of a standard Normal variable.

**(c)** With $D=\sum_{t=0}^{9}t^2=285$ and $\sigma^2=1$, the statistic is
$285(0.1373)^2\approx 5.37$. Since $5.37>3.841$, reject $H_0$ at the $5\%$ level.

**(d)** The data provide evidence that the mean echo intensity changes with time. The positive
estimated slope indicates intensifying echoes, which could signal approaching orcs and increasing
danger. A negative slope would indicate fading echoes.

</details>
